title: Reading a Source: HIPP
short: Ask four questions of any source: its Historical situation, Intended audience, Purpose and Point of view; each one shapes what the source says and leaves out.
trouble: Students summarize what a source says but never ask why it was written or for whom. A speech to supporters and a private letter by the same person can say different things for good reasons.

blocks.html: In Primary and Secondary Sources you learned to ask who made a source and when. Now go one step further. Every source was made by a person, at a moment, for someone, for a reason. Historians call this sourcing. The AP U.S. History exam asks about four parts of it, which many teachers remember as HIPP.

head: Letter
Question
Ask yourself
rows: What was going on when and where this was made?
Who was meant to read, hear or see it?
Why was it made? What did the author want to happen?
Who is the author, and how might their place in events shape what they say?

blocks.html: HIPP asks why a source says what it says. The situation, the audience, the purpose and the author's point of view shape what a source includes, what it stresses and what it leaves out.

A source is not a window onto the past; it is a message from one person to others. A general writes one way to his commander and another way to his family. Knowing the message's setting lets you use it fairly: you can trust it most on what the author was in a position to know and had little reason to bend, and read it more carefully where the author had a reason to persuade.

doc.title: From the letter of Columbus to Luis de Santángel (1493)
doc.source: Christopher Columbus, letter written on the voyage home, February to March 1493; translation in American History Leaflets (Hart and Channing), reprinted in the Harvard Classics, Volume 43
paras: … I write this to tell you how in thirty-three days I sailed to the Indies with the fleet that the illustrious King and Queen, our Sovereigns, gave me, where I discovered a great many islands, inhabited by numberless people; and of all I have taken possession for their Highnesses by proclamation and display of the Royal Standard without opposition.
They explored for three days, and found countless small communities and people, without number, but with no kind of government, so they returned.

marks.text: thirty-three days I sailed to the Indies
marks.note: Point of view: Columbus believed he had reached islands off Asia. He was wrong, but sincere.

marks.text: the illustrious King and Queen, our Sovereigns
marks.note: Audience: the letter went to a royal treasurer and was meant for Ferdinand and Isabella, who paid for the voyage.
Purpose: he stresses easy success, the kind of news that wins support for a second voyage.
Point of view: a newcomer who could not speak the language judged in a few days. Strong evidence of his view, weak evidence of Taíno life.

blocks.cap: Tap each highlighted phrase to see how HIPP applies.

blocks.title: Source the Columbus letter
blocks.q: Columbus wrote this letter on his voyage home in early 1493. Apply HIPP.
steps: H: He had just made his first crossing of the Atlantic, paid for by the Spanish crown, and needed backing for more voyages.
I: A royal treasurer, Luis de Santángel, and through him King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella.
P: To announce success and claim the lands, so the monarchs would fund him again.
P: A Genoese sailor in Spain's service, sure he had reached Asia, eager to look successful.
blocks.a: The letter is reliable about where he sailed and what he claimed, and must be read with care where it praises the riches and ease of the "Indies."

blocks.title: Audience changes tone
blocks.q: In October 1765 the Stamp Act Congress declared that colonists owed "the same allegiance to the crown" as people in Britain, and also that no taxes should be laid on them "but with their own consent." Why both?
steps: H: Parliament had just passed the Stamp Act, a direct tax on the colonies.
I: The King and both houses of Parliament.
P: To win repeal of the tax without being treated as rebels.
blocks.a: Loyal words to a powerful audience made the protest harder to dismiss. The loyalty was also real: most colonists in 1765 wanted their rights inside the empire, not independence.

doc.title: From the Declaration of Rights of the Stamp Act Congress (October 19, 1765)
doc.source: Journal of the First Congress of the American Colonies (1765), resolutions 1, 3 and 4
paras: 1st. That his majesty's subjects in these colonies, owe the same allegiance to the crown of Great Britain that is owing from his subjects born within the realm, and all due subordination to that august body, the parliament of Great Britain.

3d. That it is inseparably essential to the freedom of a people, and the undoubted rights of Englishmen, that no taxes should be imposed on them, but with their own consent, given personally, or by their representatives.
4th. That the people of these colonies are not, and from their local circumstances, cannot be represented in the house of commons in Great Britain.

marks.text: owe the same allegiance to the crown
marks.note: Audience and purpose: loyal words for the King and Parliament.
The core claim: no taxation without consent.

marks.text: cannot be represented in the house of commons
marks.note: Point of view: colonists said only their own assemblies could tax them.

blocks.html: The most common slip is to summarize a source and stop. "Columbus says he found many islands" is a summary. Sourcing asks why he wrote it that way and for whom. The opposite slip is to throw out a source because it has a point of view. Every source has one; a biased source is still evidence, at least of what its author believed or wanted others to believe.
